The analysis that shapes debate on reforms like the Milburn Review is static. It records who loses on the day the changes take effect and stops there. This tool starts from that static estimate and follows what happens next, as young people move into work, their pay rises and the economy grows.

2Moves into work

Young people moving into work, with pay and poverty paths observed in Understanding Society, net of tax and benefit withdrawal.

3Growth

The extra output of new workers, following OBR conventions, with the gain to the public finances shared out. It counts towards incomes and absolute poverty.

Starting point

On day one, the package takes around £1,000 a year from the average young person, and most from 18 and 19-year-olds

PolicyEngine’s static estimate shows how much household income each age loses when PIP and the health element of Universal Credit are withdrawn, before anyone changes what they do. Losses peak at 18 and 19 and are smallest at 16 and 17, because the package removes PIP from age 18. Averaged across all 7.5 million 16 to 24-year-olds, the loss is around £1,005 a year, or £7.5bn in total.

Source: PolicyEngine, Milburn report package, 2029-30. Average change in household income per young person, gainers and losers combined, before replacement payments.

That average hides who actually loses, which matters because only some of them can respond by moving into work.

1. Who loses

Two-thirds of the loss falls on young people already in work or education, who cannot respond by moving into work

Splitting young people into four groups shows where the loss lands. NEET young people not claiming lose nothing, the severely disabled are protected, and NEET young people who claim and lose can respond by moving into work. Young people in work or education lose most in total, but they are already working or studying. With the Youth Allowance and work allowance added back and losses phased in as claimants are reassessed, the first-year loss is the starting point for everything that follows.

From the immediate effect to living standards over time

The losses by group add up to the starting point, then moves into work and growth are layered on top.

By group, first year
Over time
Source: GGF calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and OBR conventions.

How quickly that loss is recovered depends on what young people earn once they start work.

2. What work is worth

Young people who start work see their pay rise fastest, so the gain from each job grows over time

Following young people in Understanding Society after they move into work shows that pay rises much faster for those who start young, around 50% in real terms over ten years for a 20-year-old against around 10% for someone starting at 42. Each new worker in the model follows this path, net of tax and the Universal Credit taper, so the employment effect keeps growing long after the jobs arrive.

Pay rises fastest for those who start young

Real hourly pay after entering work, entry = 100, by age at entry

Source: GGF calculations using Understanding Society.

Rising pay also lifts households out of poverty, which is where the static and long-run pictures differ most.

3. Poverty

A rise in poverty becomes a fall within a decade as young people move into work

Of young people in poverty who start work, two-thirds leave it in their first year, rising to 86% after six years in work. Each household that leaves poverty takes everyone in it out. Growth lowers absolute poverty further, but leaves relative poverty unchanged, because it lifts the poverty line along with incomes.

A rise in poverty becomes a fall as young people move into work

Change in people in poverty after housing costs, relative to no reform

Notes: Each exit counts everyone in the household. The DWP estimate is a cross-check, not used to set the model.

But the DWP’s 50,000 fall assumes every job is already filled, which raises the question of when it is actually reached.

4. Timing

How quickly young people move into work decides when poverty falls

The review phases its 440,000 extra jobs in over a decade, while the benefit changes are fully in place within around three years. If young people move into work on the review’s own timetable, poverty stays higher than without the reform for most of the first decade. If they move at the pace we observe in Understanding Society, the 50,000 fall comes around four years sooner.

The pace of moves into work decides when poverty falls

Change in relative poverty under two timetables for the same extra young people in work

Notes: DWP timetable follows the review’s NEET reduction profile, 2027/28 to 2036/37. GGF timetable follows observed moves into work in Understanding Society.

The end point is the same, but the path is not. The speed with which the Youth Guarantee and employment support reach young people matters as much to the package’s record on poverty as the benefit changes themselves, and that is something static analysis on its own cannot show.

Full Analysis of the Milburn Review

The Long-Term Effect of the Milburn Review: Counting the Future Gains from Work and Growth

The type of policy analysis produced by think tanks that influences public opinions only counts the immediate winners and losers. It rarely accounts for the second-round effects, from people moving into work and the economic growth generated. Alternative methods that consider longer run effects are too laborious to use routinely, which means reforms whose costs are immediate, but whose benefits are into the future are judged on their immediate costs alone.

This bias bears on policies that may require short term loses to generate long-term benefits, such as changes to taxes and benefits, or generally approaches to raise economic growth given these at times create some losers at the outset. Dynamic models which can capture these more wholistic effects are too complex to use by those who can wish to fit analysis within the timeframe of media attention towards a proposed reform. These are therefore reserved mostly for academics to analyse a limited number of policies often years later. The consequence is public debate is shaped only by models that by their nature can only show one side of the effect of a policy, and those able to capture total effects are unusable at the point a decision is made.

The recently announced Milburn Review is an apt demonstration of this constraint. The review seeks to get more young people into work, reduce the number of people Not in Education Employment or Training (NEET) and reform parts of the disability benefits system. Because the benefits withdrawn for some are larger than the increases in benefits for others, static analysis alone would suggest this reform is bad for people’s living standards and pushes people into poverty. It does not account for the 440,000 people swapping benefits for higher paying work1, which is the intention of the reform, nor the growth that work would generate.

This note sets out a way to close this analytical gap, applied to the 2026 Milburn Review. By borrowing long-run dynamic components and applying them to these static models, we can see that the growth this additional work generates fundamentally changes the interpretation of the reform. This approach turns an immediate loss for young people into a long term-gain, and a rise in poverty into a permanent fall within a decade.

Key findings:

  • The Milburn Review makes young people £250 per year better off once we account for its long-run effects: while the reform reduces £2bn in total in the immediate term, the effect of increased employment and the growth employment generates adds £2bn for young people in the long run.
  • While the package of reforms does raise poverty by 90,000 in the immediate term, we find it falls by 120,000 in the long-term: as young people move into work, two-thirds of those in poverty leave it in their first year, rising to 86% after six years in work.
  • The reform raises GDP by around £5bn a year once fully rolled out: and by around £22bn a year once all 440,000 young people expected to find work as a result have entered employment

1. Introduction

Statis analysis is popular amongst think tanks and government departments. While they are complex in nature, their application is straightforward and the results are easy to understand. These models change the incomes of a sample of households in response to changes to tax and benefit policies. These are static, accounting only for what is called ‘morning after effects’, meaning they capture the snapshot effect, and rarely account for behavioural responses, such as adjusting work hours, jobs etc.

Estimates of the growth effects from policy are done officially by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), but only if as part of the annual budget and is only reported if the effect of the policy is above 0.1% of potential output2. This analysis is rarely traced back to the households that bear the first-round losses.

For example, the Mirless Review in 2011 evaluated the UK tax base, and recommended abolishing and reforming the most damaging taxes, such as stamp duty3. Few of the tax reforms have been explored, which is arguably a consequence of the fact that when any potential effect of a reform is presented to the public, it’s loses would be illustrated but it’s long run effects on growth would not be. Without a practical way of showing the gains alongside the losses, the case for reform is always argued at a disadvantage.

Key term: dynamic scoring

Dynamic models include behavioural and economic responses and project these effects into the future. Static models assume nobody changes what they do, as to do so requires difficult assumptions and complex calculations. Dynamic scoring allows for people moving into work, firms investing and the economy growing as a result. These models however are involved, slow and specialist, which is why they are rarely used when UK policy is being decided.

This note sets out a way to take dynamic components from both macroeconomic and complex microsimulation models and applies them to static analysis conducted by Policy Engine of the 2026 Milburn Review. In doing so, we extend this static output out 25 years with a pseudo-dynamic macro-micro model. This work is intended to shed light on the full effects of the reforms, not as a replacement for full long-term dynamic analysis.

2. What our model does

2.1 Starting from the static estimate

Our approach starts with the policy reform of the Milburn Review, supporting documentation from the Department and Work and Pensions (DWP), and the static analysis of the reform undertaken by PolicyEngine. This gives us the number of people affected, how many return to work, the immediate cash effect broken down by group and age, and the immediate change in poverty4

We call this the immediate effect, from which we measure each long-run effect from. In a scenario where people are made worse off, this would result in a fall, after which if they’re better off over time would be a gradual rise; this is referred to as a ‘hockey stick’ graph. The static analysis gives us the first downward bend in the ‘hockey stick’.

2.2 The employment effect

The key component we add to build on this static analysis is the return to work effect on the individual. In the scenario where someone is made worse off, but enters work, we need to draw the upward trajectory in that persons standard of living (the bend upwards in the hockey stick). How steep that gradient should be requires a data driven approach to estimate.

This will naturally depend on who is affected. A younger person will have a steeper trajectory in their living standards from entering work than someone older. To map this employment effect onto different ages, we link multiple waves of Understanding Society (USOC) from 2009-10 to 2023-24 and follow people at different ages into work. This measures how often they move into work, what they earn, how their pay grows and whether their household leaves poverty as a result5. This exercise is detailed in Appendix A and the full table of results.

We cross check these results with international evidence, such as we show that 5% of a population enter work in the first year, and 56% in year 5 after a policy intervention, which aligns with Card et al (2018) who find employment effects close to zero at first and growing over two to three years6. Simarlily, we find young people on disability benefits move into work at around a quarter of the rate of those not on them (7.5% a year versus 31%), which aligns with Maestas et al (2013) who find that the return-to-work response is concentrated among people with less severe conditions7.

2.3 The growth effect

To estimate any effect on GDP is almost done with a macroeconomic model as a separate exercise to any static or dynamic tax/benefit analysis. These models are complex and built around averages (unlike tax/benefit models with have a sample of different households), meaning their application would be mostly inappropriate for this question.

We can however, in a similar way to the above, borrow dynamic components and conventions to apply to our question of turning employment growth into GDP growth. To do so, however, raises five questions. These are partly answered by OBR conventions which answers for the economy as a whole but which have not previously been answered for a specific group of households.

How much does output rise with employment?

Given the OBR frequently estimate employment effects and present the resulting effect on GDP, we can use the relationship between the two to convert our employment estimates into a GDP effect. We set this relationship using the OBR’s conventions rather than adopting a single published figure.

We first need to estimate how productive the young people effected by this package of reforms are when they enter work. Given this is a specific group of people, we cannot take the productivity level of an average worker as a macroeconomic model would naturally do, given younger people will naturally produce less at the start of their career8. If we applied average productivity levels, which is around 75k per year (gross value added of £2,497 billion divided by around 33 million people in work) that would mean 440,000 people entering work would produce 33bn in GDP per year. If we compare this to the average pay young people receive in the USOC data, which is around £15k per year, that would imply a young person entering work produces five times what they are paid. This would be problematic assumption, given studies that link firms output to workers wages find that younger workers output is associated with what they produce9.

We therefore scale productivity with pay, given we find pay of young people is around 40% of the average worker in the USOC data, which produces a more reasonable ratio of pay to output of 2.5x. This is close to previous OBR studies that assumed a typical adult entering work from inactivity is around two thirds as productive as the average worker10. Rather than hold the young persons productivity fixed at this level forever, we assume this rises over time allowing younger workers to achieve an average level of output. We let this follow the pay path we have already estimated. Firms are assumed to invest to equip them, following the OBR’s convention, so no further adjustment for capital is needed11.

We can see how this compares to other models, but comparing the ratio between a 1% rise in employment and the resulting rise in GDP. Using these above parameters, 440,000 young people is 1.3% of the workforce, who produce £17bn of output on entry, which is around 0.6%, a ratio of around 1:0.45 between the rise in employment and the rise in GDP, increasing to around 1:0.6 by year ten as their output grows with experience and the gain reaches around £22bn a year.

This is close to the relationship we can see between employment and GDP estimated by the OBR in the 2023 document accompanying the Budget’s labour supply measures, which raised employment by 0.3% and added around 0.2% to GDP; a ratio of 1:0.6. Table 1 below provides this ratio of employment to GDP from different reports under different scenarios.

Table 1: Different Ratios of Employment to GDP

SourceCaseEmployment : GDP

Our estimate sits around the middle of this range. It is above the OBR’s costing of the November 2023 welfare package, which assumed new workers join on much lower hours and earnings than average, and below the OBR’s cases where new workers are as productive as the existing workforce and capital adjusts fully. That makes it a reasonable and cautious central case for young people entering mostly low-paid work.

The Milburn Review itself does also provide a ratio of employment to growth, of around 1:0.3, which values new workers at young people’s current earnings and applies a fixed two-thirds adjustment for capital that does not change over time. This assumption is reasonable for a single figure, but given we want to see the long-run effect we have to allow for young people to reach parity with the output of the average worker of time, given we find in the USOC data the pay of young people rises over time, reflecting increasing productivity. It also applies a short-run constraint on capital to an effect a decade away, while the OBR’s convention is that capital adjusts over the medium term. The review describes its figure as illustrative rather than a full forecast, and we treat it as a low case rather than the central one.

How much of extra output reaches households?

Naturally not every pound of GDP generated will become household income. Again, a macroeconomic model can account for this through complex relationships between work, output, taxes and benefits etc.

In our version, we can take the given labour share of income (how much of household gross income is as a share of GDP produced), which is 60% in the UK. That means we subtract 40% from the GDP generated (which removes firm profits etc.). From this we remove the new workers’ own pay given we have already counted this in the employment effect and apply taxes at 37% which is the UK’s overall tax take.

Who receives the growth, and what happens to the Exchequer gain?

Additional employment and growth generate additional tax receipts to the exchequer. For scenario analysis of this nature, it is necessary to make a judgment on ‘government solvency’. Typically, scenarios where employment increases from a single policy which the analysis is evaluating keeps solvency off, so that taxes move to distribute back any additional gain to the exchequer. This isolates the full effect of the policy, meaning it is not dependent on the fiscal stance of the time, means we prioritise keeping the government debt/deficit rule stable, and leaves future decisions of what is done with additional tax receipts to governments rather than assuming exactly what they would do with it.

How does growth affect poverty?

Given economic growth raises incomes across the population, it also raises the median income, and with it the relative poverty line which is set at 60% of the median. So however large the growth effect, it leaves the number of people in relative poverty unchanged.

Absolute poverty on the other hand holds the poverty line at 60% of the median wage, which means rising incomes driven by economic growth lifts people out of poverty as people can earn above a line that does not move with them.

3. Applying the model to the Milburn Review

To apply this approach to the Milburn Review, we start with a comprehensive static evaluation of the reforms from PolicyEngine, who find that 16 to 24-year-olds on average lose around £1,005 a year, with losses peaking at 18 and 19 due to the package removing PIP from age 18 (Figure 1).

Figure 1: On day one, losses peak at 18 and 19

Static change in household income per young person by age, Milburn Review package, £ a year, 2029-30

Notes: PolicyEngine static estimate with benefits withdrawn and no replacement payments. Gainers and losers combined.

Source: PolicyEngine

The package of reforms are varied rather than a single large intervention, meaning different groups are affected in different ways that will likely influence future choices. Therefore, we make a series of groups of young people effected, to score how the policy affects each. These are those not claiming anything, those claiming, those considered severely disabled, and young people in work or education while claiming. Those not claiming are not impacted by the benefit reforms but positively impacted by moving into work. Those claiming something who a liable to lose some benefits but be positively impacted by moving into work. Those severely disabled are not liable to lose benefits given the reforms actually increase what they’re entitled to, and are considered too disabled to work so are not liable to benefit from moving into work. Lastly, those already in work, education or training who are claiming, who will lose out from the benefits reforms and not gain from moving into work given they are already working or are already in education or training.

To score what the package gives back, we take the outputs of the Youth Allowance and Work Allowance directly from PolicyEngine (around 0.9bn a year) and make assumptions about the remaining Severe and Complex Needs Insurance, the Additional Cost Allowance and the Health and Disability Fund, given these at the time of writing have no published rates.

We do this by taking the total net saving published in the review, less of PolicyEngine’s estimates of what the package gives back, which leaves £1.25bn a year as the remaining fund left to be allocated to these programs. We allocate around £0.5bn to severely disabled NEET young people and around £0.75bn to other young people who lose out. With these included, the immediate effect of the whole package is around −£5.0bn a year once fully in place, or around £660 per young person.

Figure 2: Most of the loss falls on young people already in work or education

Immediate effect of the whole Milburn Review package by group, first year, £ a year

Notes: Losses at 59% in the first year as claimants are reassessed. Replacement payments other than the Youth Allowance are a best-guess allocation of around £1.25bn.

PolicyEngine provides a phased run for when the benefit changes will become operational, with 59% of the full loss in the first year, 84% in the second, 93% in the third and all of it from the fourth. We also must provide a phase in for the work effect, given not all 440,000 extra young people will enter work immediately. We calculate when a group of young people are likely to enter the workforce following an intervention like this in Appendix A, which does this by tracking over 13k young people through spells of being out of work and into work, measuring the share of those who enter work within five years who have done so by the end of each year since their spell began.

The review does make its own assumption for when young people enter work, which is slightly slower than our estimates (both reported below). It estimates 5% of the 440,000 enter work in the first year, 56% by year five and all by year ten.

The UK measure of poverty is measured at the household level, not individual, meaning everyone in a household fall into poverty when its combined income is below 60% of the median. So when a young person moves into work and their pay lifts the household’s income above the line, everyone in the household is lifted out of poverty. Therefore we multiply each exit by 2.4, which is the average number of people in a household for each young person in it, which keeps our count on the same basis as PolicyEngine’s static estimate.

Change in the household incomes of all 16 to 24-year-olds from the whole Milburn Review package, relative to no reform, £ a year, 2024 prices

Notes: Losses phased in over four years, 440,000 extra young people in work phased in as in the review, Exchequer gain returned to everyone.

Source: GGF Calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and OBR conventions.

The resulting effect is shown in Figure 3, which shows overall that the immediate cost substantially overstates the long-term cost to young people. While the cost peaks at around £5bn, but falls shortly fater, and that loss turns into a net benefit for the young people effected by year 13. That is impacted mostly by the 440,000 young people entering work overtime, according to when the Milburn review expects them to do so, and the growth generated that lifts the wages of those same young people who initially lost out from the package of reforms. By year 25, the total effect of the package of reforms is a net benefit to young people of 1.9bn.

The poverty estimates also reveal a divergent picture once we account for these long-run effects. In the immediate term as the reductions in benefits roll out, relative poverty rises by 178,000, but as young people move into work as a result, the rise is reversed by around year six. The DWP state that they expect relative poverty to fall by 50,000 once fully rolled out, which we predict will be achieved in year 7 if we follow their timetable for when they expect young people to enter work (however it could be sooner based on our estimates for when young people enter work, explored in Figure 5 below). Once settled, the package reduces poverty by 135,000 people.

While this is based on the more widely used relative definition of poverty (those with incomes below 60% of the median), it does mean there is no growth effect observed as described above. Economic growth raises the median income, and with it the relative poverty line, so this on its own cannot lift anyone of poverty no matter how large the increase in incomes it generates. The absolute measure of poverty, on the hand, takes the same threshold but holds it fixed over time, so growth lifts people out of it as their incomes rise above that threshold and does not at the same time influence the threshold itself. We therefore add the effect on absolute poverty below which includes the effect of economic growth which reduces the number of people in poverty even further around 193,000.

Figure 4: A rise in poverty becomes a fall as young people move into work

Notes: Each exit from poverty counts everyone in the household. Growth affects absolute poverty only. The DWP estimate is a cross-check and is not used to set the model.

3.1 When is the 50,000 fall in poverty reached?

The DWP’s estimate that the package of reforms reduces relative poverty by 50,000 ‘once the package is rolled out’, but do not specify when this will be. We can use this dynamic approach to estimate when this point will be achieved.

Figure 5 compares two timetables for when the same 440,000 enter work. Our central estimate, which we use above, follows the DWP estimates for when they expect the young people effected to enter work. According to that timetable, the fall of 50,000 people in poverty is reached in year 7. If young people instead moved into work at the pace we observe in Understanding Society data, which is slightly faster than the Milburn Review assumes, relative poverty falls below its pre-reform level within three years, and four years to achieve the estimated the 50,000 fall.

While both timetables reach the same permanent fall in poverty, according to the review’s own timetable of when people enter work, around 140,000 more people are in poverty at year four. This suggests the speed with which the Youth Guarantee and employment support reach young people matters for how fast the review is able to reduce poverty.

Figure 5: The pace of moves into work decides when poverty falls

Change in relative poverty from the whole Milburn Review package under two timetables for 440,000 extra young people moving into work

Notes: The DWP timetable follows the review’s NEET reduction profile, 2027/28 to 2036/37. The GGF timetable follows observed moves into work in Understanding Society.

Source: GGF Calculations using PolicyEngine, Understanding Society, the Milburn Review and DWP.

4. Conclusion

This briefing has demonstrated why it is often essential to evaluate policies in a more wholistic way. Reforms, like those enacted in the Milburn Review, create winners and losers in the short term, but in the long-term can made better off once we allow for the positive effects of work and the growth generated to be counted in the analysis.

The challenges this creates is beyond simple methodological constraints; it can fundamentally alter how a policy is understood. We have demonstrated in this briefing how the effect on young people can be negative in the immediate term, but positive in the long; the existing models used by think tanks and by the government themselves are only capable of highlighting the former. We find that adding the effect of work and the growth that works generates, turns a package that makes people worse off in the interim to be substantial net positive in the long run.

This aligns with the very intention of such reforms, which if intended to help people into work is likely driven by the very fact that work pays more than welfare does. If we are only able to highlight the loss of welfare and not layer this understanding with the future gains from work, we create bias in how we understand policy, tilting analysis against reforms whose costs arrive first but whose benefits arrive later, and against pro-growth measures whose gains are spread across many people rather than concentrated in a few.

A model that sets the immediate effect alongside the gains from work and growth would not decide whether a reform is right, but it would let policymakers and the public weigh both sides on equal terms. This briefing has set out a more parsimonious and realistic way to do just that.

Appendix A: Using Understanding Society Data

To project what happens once young people move into work requires longitudinal data that follows the same individual over multiple years. We link waves of Understanding Society, the UK’s largest household panel survey, from 2009-10 to 2023-24, around 466,000 person-year records.

We identify every move from not working into paid work. For each move we derive hourly pay from earnings and usual hours in 2024 prices, follow the person through later waves to measure how their pay grows relative to the economy average, and link them to their household’s income to see whether the household was in poverty before they started work and whether it left poverty afterwards, after housing costs and counting everyone in the household. Table A1 sets out the estimates the model uses.

Table A1: Estimates from Understanding Society used in the model

EstimateResult
Annual rate of moving into work, NEET 16 to 24-year-olds31% for those not on disability benefits, 7.5% for those on them
Entry pay, 18 to 24-year-olds£8.91 an hour, around 33 hours a week (2024 prices)
Pay growth above the economy average after entry4.3% a year aged 18 to 24, 2.4% aged 25 to 34, under 1% from 35
In household poverty before entering work, 18 to 2433% after housing costs
Out of poverty after entering work, 18 to 2466% after one year in work, rising to 86% after six

Figure A1 shows that young people who enter work see their pay rise much faster than those who enter later, around 50% in real terms over ten years for a 20-year-old against around 10% for someone entering at 42, and each new worker in the model follows the path for their age, net of tax and the Universal Credit taper. Figure A2 shows the share of young people in poverty who are out of it by years in work. Beyond six years, where our data run out, the model lets this share rise slowly towards the 87% observed for all workers aged 25 to 34, closing 39% of the remaining gap each year, the rate at which people in poverty typically leave it.
